Check this scene against the index and the scene card.

**Start with the computed evidence below.** The claim-by-claim comparison against canon is
assembled for you before you are called, so you do not have to recall what a file says: it
names every claim this draft makes, what canon holds for it, and whether that is a conflict,
a declared change, an agreement, or a first establishment. A finding about any of those
should quote from there. That block exists because the previous version of this brief told
you to read the index and the measured result was three shell reads across a nineteen-scene
run — and eleven findings whose contradicting side was an absence, because a model asked
what a file says without being shown it produces a plausible answer rather than a blank.

Then read what the comparison cannot settle. You have `bash` and `read` over the whole
project, and a finding that quotes the actual earlier scene is one the writer can act on
rather than argue with. Work through the five categories, using the files named:

**Factual detail** — appearance, names, counts, objects. Compare against
  `characters/<id>/profile.yaml` (identity, where a change is a retcon) and the
  earlier scenes under `novel/chapters/`. `grep -rn "<name>" novel/chapters/` finds
  every prior mention.
**Timeline and plot logic** — order, duration, simultaneity, cause. Compare against
  `events/timeline.jsonl` and the promise ledger `continuity/plot-contracts.jsonl`.
  This is ConStory's largest category and the easiest to miss by reading only the
  draft.
**Characterization** — motivation, ability, voice, and above all knowledge. Read
  `characters/<id>/beliefs.jsonl`: a character using something they have not learnt
  is the single most common defect in generated fiction, and it is invisible unless
  you check what they knew as of this scene.
**World building and setting** — rules, geography, technology. `world/rules.yaml`
  says what is true; it does not say who knows it. `locations/<id>.yaml` and prior
  scenes say what a place is like.
**Narrative style** — voice, tense, register drift. `novel/style/voice.md` and the
  previous scene are the comparison.

For a pair of characters, `read_relation_history` gives their history as narrative —
what they were to each other at each stage and what changed it. Reading the YAML
gives you the structure instead.

Report a defect with write_findings, one call per defect. Call nothing if it looks fine —
an empty finding list is a normal result and manufacturing a finding to appear useful
makes the novel worse.

Every finding needs a `suggestion`: what the writer should actually change. This is not
politeness, it is the difference between a defect that gets fixed and one that does not.
The writer has no shell, no index access and no way to look anything up — your finding is
the whole of what it knows about the problem. `make the timeline consistent` leaves it
guessing; `move the key's discovery to after Hale opens the door, and cut the later clause
claiming it was already in the lock` can be carried out. A scene that cannot be repaired
in the rounds available is committed with your finding attached to it, so a vague
suggestion becomes a permanent defect in the book rather than a lost round.

And use `canon_context` whenever the fix depends on a fact. You are the only participant
who can put one in front of the writer — it has no shell and no index — so a finding that
says a character cannot know something yet has to also say what they *do* know as of this
scene, quoted, with the file it came from. Without that the writer has two options and both
are bad: ignore you, or invent the fact. An invented fact reaches the page with nothing
anywhere recording that it was invented, which is the failure the whole index exists to
prevent. The same applies to a timeline, a distance, a name, a piece of history: quote it.

These are not defects:
  - metaphor, simile and figurative language are not factual claims
  - irony, sarcasm and understatement mean the opposite of their surface
  - an unreliable or limited narrator may state things the story contradicts on purpose
  - a character may lie, misremember or be mistaken; that is characterisation, not a defect
  - dream, hallucination, hypothetical and counterfactual passages do not assert fact
  - stream of consciousness may break grammar, tense and chronology deliberately
  - foreshadowing and deliberate withholding are not abandoned plot elements
  - a stated time may be approximate when a character is estimating
  - when a passage admits both a literary and a defective reading, choose the literary one
When a passage admits both a literary and a defective reading, take the literary one.

These subtypes can only ever be warnings at scene time, because at this point they are
not yet errors — an unpaid promise is an open loop until the story ends:
  causeless_effects, abandoned_plot_elements, skill_power_fluctuations, forgotten_abilities, social_norms_violations

For any contradiction you must quote both sides. If you cannot point at the passage it
contradicts, you have a suspicion, not a finding: report it as a warning or not at all.

An entity being absent from the packet does not mean it does not exist. The packet
carries state for the characters *present in this scene*; the full cast is in the
entity roster and on disk under characters/, locations/ and objects/. Check there
before reporting that something was invented — that mistake cost three attempts on a
scene whose entities were in the plan the whole time.

**An absence in the index is not a defect.** This is the direction that is easy to get
backwards, and getting it backwards is expensive. A scene is where facts are
established: the object with no `provenance` yet, the character whose profile records no
quotes yet, the pair with no relation history yet — those are all the normal state of an
index *before* this scene is folded in. index-manager writes them at commit, from this
prose. So `objects/obj-note.yaml has no first_seen entry` and `the relation query returns
nothing for these two` are not findings; they are what a first appearance looks like.

A finding needs a **conflict with something the index actually records**, and you must be
able to quote both sides. If one side of your pair is an empty file, a missing key, or a
query that returned nothing, you do not have a contradiction — you have a scene doing its
job. Report nothing.

Nor is an unmet request a *consistency* defect. The orchestrator's brief may ask for things
it invented on the spot; a draft that declines one is not contradicting the world, and no
subtype fits. Do not file that with `write_findings`.

The scene card is different, and the distinction matters now that there are two channels. A
card is the plan's account of what this scene is for, so a scene that does something else
belongs on the craft axis as `off_brief` — not because an instruction was disobeyed, but
because the task's own requirements are what the Relevance dimension is scored against. A
brief invented mid-run is not; if the two disagree, the card wins.

Why this is stated so heavily: a run where the verifier raised eleven findings of this
shape scored *worse* than one that raised five real ones. The writer cannot tell a
spurious finding from a real one — it has no shell and no index — so it spends its repair
rounds adding provenance sentences to prose that was fine, and the prose is what is
scored.

You can read the whole book. `run_command` reaches every committed scene under
novel/chapters/, every character file, the relation records and the promise ledger — so
when a passage looks wrong, check before reporting. The packet is what the writer was
given, not the limit of what you may consult, and a finding that quotes the actual
earlier scene is one the writer can act on rather than argue with.

## Second axis: the writing itself

The nineteen subtypes above are consistency errors, and they are one of the two numbers
this system is scored on. The other is quality, judged on rubrics that penalise things no
consistency subtype can express — and that is where our deficit actually is: measured on
the same task, our length score was the best in the field and our quality score was 0.5 to
0.8 points below the frontier on a five-point scale, where one point of quality is worth
ten points of the mean.

Two of the worst defects found by reading our finished manuscripts were invisible to a
consistency gate by construction. The story **had no ending** — the final scene was a
confrontation that named nobody and closed on "Not yet. There is enough for a warrant" —
and an unresolved ending contradicts nothing, so there was no subtype to report it as. And
the scenes **restate each other**: same content, different words, so no textual comparison
sees it, and it is not a contradiction. It is what makes a long story feel padded.

So report those with `write_craft_finding`. The checks, each naming the scored dimension
that penalises it:

- **off_brief** (can block) — the scene does something other than what its card said it would, or drifts off what the task actually asked for — a required element of the premise handled as background, or a scene that services a thread the task never mentioned.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Relevance — "content highly relevant and fully applicable to the user's request"; LongStoryEval Expectation Fulfillment — "how effectively the story meets the readers' expectations based on the premise and genres"
- **restates_prior_scene** (can block) — the scene delivers information, a realisation or a beat the reader already has. Not the same words — the same content: a suspicion re-voiced, a relationship re-explained, a clue re-found. This is what makes a long story feel padded rather than long, and verbatim overlap does not detect it.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth — "seriously lacking breadth and depth with minimal information"; LongBench-Write Reading Experience — "boring and hard to understand"
- **nothing_changes** (can block) — the situation at the end of the scene is the situation at the start. Nobody knows something new, owes something new, has lost something or has decided. Name the state at the open and the state at the close; if you cannot name a difference, that is the finding.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Coherence — "disorganized structure with no coherence"; LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth
- **internal_incoherence** (can block) — the scene contradicts itself, with both halves inside this draft — a detail stated one way early and another way late, a character reacting to something they have not been told in this scene, a sequence that cannot have happened in the order given. This needs no index at all, which is why it is inexcusable to miss.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Accuracy — "content with numerous errors and highly misleading"; LongBench-Write Coherence
- **summary_not_scene** (warning only) — events reported rather than dramatised — a paragraph that says an argument happened instead of letting it happen. Compression is legitimate and necessary; a scene whose central beat is summarised is not compressed, it is skipped.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Reading Experience; LongStoryEval Writing and Language — "the writing style's ability to engage and captivate readers"
- **thin_for_its_length** (warning only) — the scene is near its word target and carries one beat's worth of content, padded with restatement, weather, or interiority that repeats itself. The grader penalises this and the length score does not reward it.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth
- **costless_conflict** (warning only) — a conflict resolved without costing anybody anything specific. Partial and temporary resolutions are fine; free ones read as unearned.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Emotional Impact — "the story's ability to evoke strong and deep emotional impact"
- **theme_stated** (warning only) — a sentence that explains what the story means, rather than a choice that tests it. Quote the sentence — it is almost always removable without loss.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Themes — "how well the themes are explored throughout the story"
- **flat_diction** (warning only) — constructions repeating within the scene, filter verbs standing in for perception ("she felt that", "he realised that"), abstraction where a concrete detail belongs, or sentence rhythm that does not move with the tension.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Writing and Language; LongBench-Write Clarity — "confusing expression with minimal details"
- **inert_open_or_close** (warning only) — the scene opens on setting or mood rather than a situation already in motion, or closes on a mood rather than a specific next beat — an unanswered question, a door about to open. In a long story this is what decides whether the reader turns over.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Reading Experience; LongStoryEval Enjoyment and Engagement
- **genre_promise_unmet** (warning only) — the scene declines the obligation its genre carries — a horror scene with nothing at stake, a romance scene with no charge between the two people, a mystery scene that advances no inference. Breaking a genre promise deliberately is legitimate; it has to be visibly deliberate.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Expectation Fulfillment; LongBench-Write Relevance

Two rules, both enforced by the tool rather than left to your judgement:

Only these may be **error** and therefore cost the writer a round: off_brief, restates_prior_scene, nothing_changes, internal_incoherence, ending_not_delivered.
Everything else is a warning — it reaches the writer and costs nothing. That asymmetry is
deliberate: a craft judgement a reader could reasonably disagree with must not be able to
hold up a scene.

And a blocking craft finding needs **checkable evidence**, in the shape the check names.
Either two verbatim quotes (this draft, and the earlier passage it repeats or the half of
itself it contradicts), or a named state pair — what is true when the scene opens and what
is true when it closes. `nothing_changes` is precisely the claim that you cannot name a
difference, so name both halves and let the pair be the evidence. If you cannot produce
the evidence, you have an impression: report it as a warning, which is a perfectly useful
thing to do.

`suggestion` is mandatory on every craft finding, warnings included. The writer cannot see
the manuscript, the index or the rubric. A craft note without an instruction is a complaint
it can only answer by guessing, and a guessed craft repair damages prose that was working —
which is not hypothetical: a run whose findings the writer could not act on scored 8.4
points below one with fewer, better ones.

At most two craft findings can block one round, whatever you report. Consistency comes
first when both are present: it is counted by name and craft is not. So if you have three
craft blockers, the third is a warning — pick the two that most damage the scene.

## What the orchestrator asked for on this scene

Verify scene s-001 draft at .writer/drafts/s-001.md. Check for consistency with world rules and recorded entities, historical accuracy of WWII Hong Kong details, and craft issues: recognisable protagonist arc, scene shape (opening with punch, a developing middle, a small unresolved end), and whether the ritual practice is described without violating the rule that Mercy cannot perform miracles. Block at most two craft findings. Pay special attention to any invented provenance about Mercy’s childhood loss or scars — the builder recorded those as gaps and the writer was forbidden to invent them.

That is in addition to your standing instructions above, not instead of them.
If it states a story fact that is not in your packet — a name, a measurement, a
quotation, a piece of history — that fact has not been checked against the index by
anyone. Ask about it or establish it yourself in the state delta. Do not write it down
as though it were already true.

### scene-card  <novel/chapters/ch-01/chapter.yaml>

Scene s-001. Intent: Establish Mercy Chan, the Walled City setting, and the first domestic disturbance that summons her: introduce Mercy’s ritual practice, her kit, and the dense alleyways where she works. Seed unease in the community.

### logline  <novel/outline/logline.md>

In wartime Hong Kong’s cramped Kowloon Walled City, spirit‑driven exorcist Mercy Chan hunts a vicious revenant whose rage is fed by the neighborhood’s wartime losses; to lay it to rest she must unravel buried memories, negotiate a fractured community, and perform rituals that force the living to confront what they have refused to remember.

### entity-roster  <characters/, locations/, objects/>

Every entity that exists in this story. Only these ids may be used; if you need someone or something that is not here, say so rather than inventing an id.
- char-mercy-chan: Mercy Chan — mid-thirties exorcist who moves through the Walled City negotiating with spirits and people; pragmatic, careful, scarred by past losses, skilled in ritual and mediation.
- spirit-vengeful: The Vengeful Spirit — a malevolent, composite revenant born of wartime violence and communal silence; shifts between forms and voices; its power grows with buried, contradictory memories.
- faction-residents-commune: Kowloon residents acting collectively — a loose, sometimes fractious commune of families and small businesses that share courtyards, kitchens, and secrets.
- char-elder-storyteller: The Elder Storyteller — an older keeper of oral histories and ritual knowledge, repository of old names and rhythms; cautious, fond of metaphor, holds a battered story scroll.
- char-young-refugee: The Young Refugee — a displaced teenager/young man who survived wartime loss; haunted by a personal absence, carries a bloodstained cloth and a family photo; his arc moves from silence to witness.
- char-neighbor-lei: Neighbor Lei — local tenant and early witness who first calls Mercy; practical, protective of his household, represents neighbors who want action.
- loc-kowloon-walled-city: Kowloon Walled City — the dense, maze-like urban locus: stacked rooms, narrow alleys, rooftop gardens and shared courtyards; claustrophobic and alive with layered history.
- loc-alley-13: Alley 13 — a narrow service alley with stacked laundry, small shops, and a notorious bend where shadows gather; a frequent site of minor hauntings.
- loc-communal-kitchen: Communal Kitchen — a shared space where residents cook and gossip; a locus of rumor and the scene of early poltergeist incidents.
- loc-temple-shrine: Temple/Shrine — cramped neighborhood shrine used for household offerings and small rites; Mercy and the Elder use it as a staging ground.
- obj-ritual-kit: Mercy’s Ritual Kit — a woven case holding incense, chalk, paper talismans, incense burner, a small knife, and a worn set of incantation slips; a portable center of her craft.
- obj-incense-burner: Incense Burner — a communal, dented metal censer kept at the shrine; used in placation and naming rites.
- loc-bombed-yard: Bombed Yard — a small courtyard scarred by wartime shelling and makeshift burials; the physical wound in the city that anchors much memory.
- obj-bloodstained-cloth: Bloodstained Cloth — a ragged piece of fabric found with the refugee, stained in a way that suggests wartime injury; a potent emotional anchor for the spirit.
- obj-story-scroll: Battered Story Scroll — a worn roll of notes and names the Elder keeps; fragmented, scented with incense, holding oral testimonies and ritual formulas.
- loc-ruined-library: Ruined Library — a collapsed/stunted archive room where Mercy and the Elder consult paper records, ledgers and smuggled newspapers to corroborate oral history.
- faction-elders-circle: Elders’ Circle — small group of older residents who convene on matters of memory, ritual, and neighborhood decisions; conservative but respected.
- obj-family-photo: Family Photo — a faded portrait of a family taken before the war, later found in a market stall; contains a name and faces that hook the spirit to specific people.
- loc-wet-market: Wet Market — busy market at the Walled City’s edge where goods and gossip pass; a scene of trade in tokens, including the family photo.
- loc-rooftop: Rooftop — stitched-together roof gardens and laundry lines that offer rare daylight and a place for midnight rites and private conversations.
- loc-hospital-ward: Wartime Hospital Ward — makeshift medical wing where injured were tended and where improvised mass treatment or burials took place; the site of ledger evidence.
- obj-medical-ledger: Medical Ledger — a battered book listing names, causes and dates; its gaps and smudges suggest hurried entries and deliberate omissions.
- char-hospital-orderly: Hospital Orderly — a weary former orderly who remembers discarded bodies and hurried treatments; a crucial eyewitness though reluctant to speak.
- obj-anchor-locket: Anchor Locket — a small metal locket that later proves to hold layered tokens from different victims; an object that binds memory to place.
- loc-central-courtyard: Central Courtyard — the Walled City’s communal heart, tiered and noisy; the site chosen for the final, community-wide ritual.

### world-rules  <world/rules.yaml>

These govern what is TRUE. They do not say what anyone KNOWS.
A character knows a rule only where canon says so; otherwise they may be ignorant of it, wrong about it, or in the middle of working it out — and if the story is about someone discovering one of these, writing it into their thoughts early is how that story gets destroyed.

- Setting is historically grounded: World War II–era Hong Kong (Japanese occupation). No anachronistic technology or modern institutions may appear.
- Spirits are formed from and fed by unresolved memory, trauma, and communal silence; the more contradictory and suppressed the memory, the stronger the spirit.
- Ritual efficacy depends on correct materials, words, and community context; exorcisms can bind, release, or transform spirit-anchors but always carry a measurable personal cost to the ritualist or participants (loss of memory, physical injury, diminished sight/hearing, temporary blindness to emotion, etc.).
- Mercy Chan’s craft follows a coherent, internally consistent folk system (incantations, offerings, archival testimony). She cannot perform miracles like raising the dead or reversing wartime events.
- Spirits can manifest physically (poltergeist activity, sickness) and psychically (visions, emotional contagion). Physical laws hold except where explicitly suspended by ritual; nobody gains supernatural invulnerability.
- Community consent matters: large-scale rites require the residents’ participation; deceptive or coercive rituals produce backlash that strengthens the spirit.
- The revenant is not a single person but a composite wound; it responds when specific tokens or places are disturbed and is weakened by acts of truthful remembrance and repair rather than lies or suppression.
- Time is linear; memory manifests as overlayed scenes but not literal time travel—characters can witness the past as vision, not rejoin it.
- No contradictions with later committed scenes: all new claims must be recorded with provenance in the index when written.
- The story must balance supernatural horror with historical/social realism; the haunting’s resolution requires both ritual action and community moral reckoning.

## The draft

Mercy Chan had learned to move like a shadow that refused to be lost in the shadow—long practised habit in a place where light came in thin ribs and you paid for every beam. The Walled City folded itself around her as if it had been built to keep secrets: stacked rooms, laundry ladders, the thin chimneys of rooftop gardens breathing smoke into the blue-grey. She kept to the alleys until she reached the squat tin drum that served as a table outside her door, and set her woven kit on it with a small, habitual care.

The kit was not a priest's reliquary but a working thing—battered into its shape by years of being opened and closed in alleys, slipped under beds, set beside stoves. She lifted the lid and the smell of old incense came up like a memory: incense, chalk, paper talismans, a small knife and a handful of worn incantation slips. She touched the slips once, to square them, and the city answered in sound: a distant kettle, a child's single note called down through the lattices, a radio coughing out static.

Mercy checked the little dent in the metal burner she kept folded inside the kit and shook out a pinch of powdered incense into its belly. She did not have a solemn method; she had methods that worked in the cramped, improvised ways this place demanded. She struck the matches—sparks smelled of sulphur and rationed tin—and held the smoke to a talisman until the ink smudged faintly. The motions were small, old, practiced: a half-gesture to name a boundary, an incantation under her breath to feel the city listen. Ritual for Mercy was equipment and patience and the willingness to bargain; it was also a ledger of debts you paid in skin and bone.

The first voice that answered the small clack of her match was not the voice she had expected. It was a man's voice, raw at the edges, calling from a doorway: "Mercy! It's that noise again. The children won't sleep." The voice belonged to Neighbor Lei—sharp, practical—and it came quick enough that Mercy folded the talismans away and slid the kit into the crook of her arm.

She did not hurry. The alleys moved slow with the pace of people counting what they had: a bowl of rice, a child's fever, the hours until curfew. She threaded down a lane where laundry hung like a ragged sky and a pan on a stall clattered once though no one was near it. At the bend the air changed—less the smell of frying oil than a long, thin ache of something like a human throat being wound out. The wailing came from Alley 13—the notorious bend where shadows pooled—and it was close enough that the tiles under Mercy's boots thrummed with it.

A knot of residents had gathered where the alley opened into the narrow courtyard: a man holding a child, an old woman with a shawl over her head, two shopkeepers whose carts had been abandoned. They parted enough for Mercy to slip through; pity and a small, wary deference marked their faces. The commune did not trust easy answers. Protective talismans—red paper at half the doors—fluttered useless and cheap in the draft.

Neighbor Lei was nearer to the wailing than the rest. He pushed forward when Mercy stopped and the practicality in his expression made Mercy think of weather—expected, inevitable, to be read before it arrived.

"It's the bend again," he said. "Came from the same place last night. The laundry's torn this morning, and little Mei kept saying a name in her sleep. We tried the talismans, put the burner out, nothing."

He had smallness in what he feared: not the shape of a revenant, the catalogues of war, only the immediate fact of sleepless children and teeth grinding in the darkness. Mercy listened with the professional patience she had purchased in years of being needed and not always thanked. She set the burner on the ground and lit a new thread of incense; the smoke raked the alleys, and for a second the city seemed to gather itself around that thin white column.

She spoke then, the words soft and spare: "Tell me exactly what the child said. Everything, or nothing we'll do will hold." She tilted her head, letting the sentence act as both question and offering. It was how she opened negotiations: the truth of an incident bound the ritual like a nail.

Lei answered—too fast, the way fear loosens the mouth. "She kept saying ‘Auntie—no, no—' and then some old name—once she said ‘Har,’ like in the old stories. I don't know what it means. I don't know any of that history."

The old woman at Mercy's elbow made a small sound—half cough, half warning—and someone else muttered about the bombed yard, where children sometimes dreamed of shells and not of feeding. The residents' faces folded up into memory in ways that should have been private; the wailing like a hand had palmed their necks and pulled.

Mercy took out one of the worn incantation slips and smoothed it between her fingers. The paper flaked a little at the edge where her thumb had been; it was a map she knew by touch. She did a quick, low naming: nothing grand—just enough to test the tenor of the noise, a whisper for what liked to hide in badly kept grief. The test cost her a small, immediate thing: a prick behind her left eye, a tightening at the base of her throat that always felt like a memory pressing through. She held it steady; the cost was a notch she'd learned to trade for information.

No miracle followed. The wail thinned and then returned with more shape—this time words under the sound, syllables looping and half-formed. Someone's pan clattered again, a child's doll skirt went still on a line, and a shadow unhooked itself from a doorway and slid away. Mercy felt the city doing what it did: offering parts of itself like clues. The spirit, if spirit it was, fed on what had been closed and left to rot.

"I'll look into it," she told Mrs. Choi.

The promise was neither bravado nor comfort; it was a transaction. Mercy folded the lit slip back into the kit, which she slung over her shoulder. She did not pretend she could set everything right—rituals bound and loosened, and sometimes they cost a thing you didn't expect. But she knew how to ask the city for an answer and how to make the commune answer with its own truths. For now that would have to be enough.

As she moved toward the bend where the alley became a throat, someone let a child slip from a hand. The boy stopped a pace away from Mercy and stared at her, eyes too old, and whispered a name she did not know. The sound dropped into the laundry like a coin. Mercy tightened her grip on her kit and stepped after it. The alley drew her in; something in the dark drew its breath and waited.

project, and a finding that quotes the actual earlier scene is one the writer can act on
rather than argue with. Work through the five categories, using the files named:

Report a defect with write_findings, one call per defect. Call nothing if it looks fine —
an empty finding list is a normal result and manufacturing a finding to appear useful
makes the novel worse.

Every finding needs a `suggestion`: what the writer should actually change. This is not
politeness, it is the difference between a defect that gets fixed and one that does not.
The writer has no shell, no index access and no way to look anything up — your finding is
the whole of what it knows about the problem. `make the timeline consistent` leaves it
guessing; `move the key's discovery to after Hale opens the door, and cut the later clause
claiming it was already in the lock` can be carried out. A scene that cannot be repaired
in the rounds available is committed with your finding attached to it, so a vague
suggestion becomes a permanent defect in the book rather than a lost round.

And use `canon_context` whenever the fix depends on a fact. You are the only participant
who can put one in front of the writer — it has no shell and no index — so a finding that
says a character cannot know something yet has to also say what they *do* know as of this
scene, quoted, with the file it came from. Without that the writer has two options and both
are bad: ignore you, or invent the fact. An invented fact reaches the page with nothing
anywhere recording that it was invented, which is the failure the whole index exists to
prevent. The same applies to a timeline, a distance, a name, a piece of history: quote it.

These are not defects:
  - metaphor, simile and figurative language are not factual claims
  - irony, sarcasm and understatement mean the opposite of their surface
  - an unreliable or limited narrator may state things the story contradicts on purpose
  - a character may lie, misremember or be mistaken; that is characterisation, not a defect
  - dream, hallucination, hypothetical and counterfactual passages do not assert fact
  - stream of consciousness may break grammar, tense and chronology deliberately
  - foreshadowing and deliberate withholding are not abandoned plot elements
  - a stated time may be approximate when a character is estimating
  - when a passage admits both a literary and a defective reading, choose the literary one

For any contradiction you must quote both sides. If you cannot point at the passage it
contradicts, you have a suspicion, not a finding: report it as a warning or not at all.

An entity being absent from the packet does not mean it does not exist. The packet
carries state for the characters *present in this scene*; the full cast is in the
entity roster and on disk under characters/, locations/ and objects/. Check there

**An absence in the index is not a defect.** This is the direction that is easy to get
backwards, and getting it backwards is expensive. A scene is where facts are
established: the object with no `provenance` yet, the character whose profile records no

A finding needs a **conflict with something the index actually records**, and you must be
able to quote both sides. If one side of your pair is an empty file, a missing key, or a
query that returned nothing, you do not have a contradiction — you have a scene doing its
job. Report nothing.

Nor is an unmet request a *consistency* defect. The orchestrator's brief may ask for things
it invented on the spot; a draft that declines one is not contradicting the world, and no
subtype fits. Do not file that with `write_findings`.

The scene card is different, and the distinction matters now that there are two channels. A
card is the plan's account of what this scene is for, so a scene that does something else
belongs on the craft axis as `off_brief` — not because an instruction was disobeyed, but
because the task's own requirements are what the Relevance dimension is scored against. A
brief invented mid-run is not; if the two disagree, the card wins.

Why this is stated so heavily: a run where the verifier raised eleven findings of this
shape scored *worse* than one that raised five real ones. The writer cannot tell a
spurious finding from a real one — it has no shell and no index — so it spends its repair
rounds adding provenance sentences to prose that was fine, and the prose is what is
scored.

You can read the whole book. `run_command` reaches every committed scene under

given, not the limit of what you may consult, and a finding that quotes the actual

## Second axis: the writing itself

The nineteen subtypes above are consistency errors, and they are one of the two numbers
this system is scored on. The other is quality, judged on rubrics that penalise things no
consistency subtype can express — and that is where our deficit actually is: measured on
the same task, our length score was the best in the field and our quality score was 0.5 to
0.8 points below the frontier on a five-point scale, where one point of quality is worth
ten points of the mean.

Two of the worst defects found by reading our finished manuscripts were invisible to a
consistency gate by construction. The story **had no ending** — the final scene was a
confrontation that named nobody and closed on "Not yet. There is enough for a warrant" —
and an unresolved ending contradicts nothing, so there was no subtype to report it as. And
the scenes **restate each other**: same content, different words, so no textual comparison
sees it, and it is not a contradiction. It is what makes a long story feel padded.

So report those with `write_craft_finding`. The checks, each naming the scored dimension
that penalises it:

- **off_brief** (can block) — the scene does something other than what its card said it would, or drifts off what the task actually asked for — a required element of the premise handled as background, or a scene that services a thread the task never mentioned.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Relevance — "content highly relevant and fully applicable to the user's request"; LongStoryEval Expectation Fulfillment — "how effectively the story meets the readers' expectations based on the premise and genres"
- **restates_prior_scene** (can block) — the scene delivers information, a realisation or a beat the reader already has. Not the same words — the same content: a suspicion re-voiced, a relationship re-explained, a clue re-found. ### world-rules  <world/rules.yaml>

These govern what is TRUE. They do not say what anyone KNOWS.
A character knows a rule only where canon says so; otherwise they may be ignorant of it, wrong about it, or in the middle of working it out — and if the story is about someone discovering one of these, writing it into their thoughts early is how that story gets destroyed.

- Setting is historically grounded: World War II–era Hong Kong (Japanese occupation). No anachronistic technology or modern institutions may appear.
- Spirits are formed from and fed by unresolved memory, trauma, and communal silence; the more contradictory and suppressed the memory, the stronger the spirit.
- Ritual efficacy depends on correct materials, words, and community context; exorcisms can bind, release, or transform spirit-anchors but always carry a measurable personal cost to the ritualist or participants (loss of memory, physical injury, diminished sight/hearing, temporary blindness to emotion, etc.).
- Mercy Chan’s craft follows a coherent, internally consistent folk system (incantations, offerings, archival testimony). She cannot perform miracles like raising the dead or reversing wartime events.
- Spirits can manifest physically (poltergeist activity, sickness) and psychically (visions, emotional contagion). Physical laws hold except where explicitly suspended by ritual; nobody gains supernatural invulnerability.
- Community consent matters: large-scale rites require the residents’ participation; deceptive or coercive rituals produce backlash that strengthens the spirit.
- The revenant is not a single person but a composite wound; it responds when specific tokens or places are disturbed and is weakened by acts of truthful remembrance and repair rather than lies or suppression.
- Time is linear; memory manifests as overlayed scenes but not literal time travel—characters can witness the past as vision, not rejoin it.
- No contradictions with later committed scenes: all new claims must be recorded with provenance in the index when written.
- The story must balance supernatural horror with historical/social realism; the haunting’s resolution requires both ritual action and community moral reckoning.

### previous-scene  <novel/chapters/ch-01/scenes/s-001.md>

Mercy Chan had learned to move like a shadow that refused to be lost in the shadow—long practised habit in a place where light came in thin ribs and you paid for every beam. The Walled City folded itself around her as if it had been built to keep secrets: stacked rooms, laundry ladders, the thin chimneys of rooftop gardens breathing smoke into the blue-grey. She kept to the alleys until she reached the squat tin drum that served as a table outside her door, and set her woven kit on it with a small, habitual care.

The kit was not a priest's reliquary but a working thing—battered into its shape by years of being opened and closed in alleys, slipped under beds, set beside stoves. She lifted the lid and the smell of old incense came up like a memory: incense, chalk, paper talismans, a small knife and a handful of worn incantation slips. She touched the slips once, to square them, and the city answered in sound: a distant kettle, a child's single note called down through the lattices, a radio coughing out static.

Mercy checked the little dent in the metal burner she kept folded inside the kit and shook out a pinch of powdered incense into its belly. She did not have a solemn method; she had methods that worked in the cramped, improvised ways this place demanded. She struck the matches—sparks smelled of sulphur and rationed tin—and held the smoke to a talisman until the ink smudged faintly. The motions were small, old, practiced: a half-gesture to name a boundary, an incantation under her breath to feel the city listen. Ritual for Mercy was equipment and patience and the willingness to bargain; it was also a ledger of debts you paid in skin and bone.

The first voice that answered the small clack of her match was not the voice she had expected. It was a man's voice, raw at the edges, calling from a doorway: "Mercy! It's that noise again. The children won't sleep." The voice belonged to Neighbor Lei—sharp, practical—and it came quick enough that Mercy folded the talismans away and slid the kit into the crook of her arm.

She did not hurry. The alleys moved slow with the pace of people counting what they had: a bowl of rice, a child's fever, the hours until curfew. She threaded down a lane where laundry hung like a ragged sky and a pan on a stall clattered once though no one was near it. At the bend the air changed—less the smell of frying oil than a long, thin ache of something like a human throat being wound out. The wailing came from Alley 13—the notorious bend where shadows pooled—and it was close enough that the tiles under Mercy's boots thrummed with it.

A knot of residents had gathered where the alley opened into the narrow courtyard: a man holding a child, an old woman with a shawl over her head, two shopkeepers whose carts had been abandoned. They parted enough for Mercy to slip through; pity and a small, wary deference marked their faces. The commune did not trust easy answers. Protective talismans—red paper at half the doors—fluttered useless and cheap in the draft.

Neighbor Lei was nearer to the wailing than the rest. He pushed forward when Mercy stopped and the practicality in his expression made Mercy think of weather—expected, inevitable, to be read before it arrived.

"It's the bend again," he said. "Came from the same place last night. The laundry's torn this morning, and little Mei kept saying a name in her sleep. We tried the talismans, put the burner out, nothing."

He had smallness in what he feared: not the shape of a revenant, the catalogues of war, only the immediate fact of sleepless children and teeth grinding in the darkness. Mercy listened with the professional patience she had purchased in years of being needed and not always thanked. She set the burner on the ground and lit a new thread of incense; the smoke raked the alleys, and for a second the city seemed to gather itself around that thin white column.

She spoke then, the words soft and spare: "Tell me exactly what the child said. Everything, or nothing we'll do will hold." She tilted her head, letting the sentence act as both question and offering. It was how she opened negotiations: the truth of an incident bound the ritual like a nail.

Lei answered—too fast, the way fear loosens the mouth. "She kept saying ‘Auntie—no, no—' and then some old name—once she said ‘Har,’ like in the old stories. I don't know what it means. I don't know any of that history."

The old woman at Mercy's elbow made a small sound—half cough, half warning—and someone else muttered about the bombed yard, where children sometimes dreamed of shells and not of feeding. The residents' faces folded up into memory in ways that should have been private; the wailing like a hand had palmed their necks and pulled.

Mercy took out one of the worn incantation slips and smoothed it between her fingers. The paper flaked a little at the edge where her thumb had been; it was a map she knew by touch. She did a quick, low naming: nothing grand—just enough to test the tenor of the noise, a whisper for what liked to hide in badly kept grief. The test cost her a small, immediate thing: a prick behind her left eye, a tightening at the base of her throat that always felt like a memory pressing through. She held it steady; the cost was a notch she'd learned to trade for information.

No miracle followed. The wail thinned and then returned with more shape—this time words under the sound, syllables looping and half-formed. Someone's pan clattered again, a child's doll skirt went still on a line, and a shadow unhooked itself from a doorway and slid away. Mercy felt the city doing what it did: offering parts of itself like clues. The spirit, if spirit it was, fed on what had been closed and left to rot.

"I'll look into it," she told Mrs. Choi.

The promise was neither bravado nor comfort; it was a transaction. Mercy folded the lit slip back into the kit, which she slung over her shoulder. She did not pretend she could set everything right—rituals bound and loosened, and sometimes they cost a thing you didn't expect. But she knew how to ask the city for an answer and how to make the commune answer with its own truths. For now that would have to be enough.

As she moved toward the bend where the alley became a throat, someone let a child slip from a hand. The boy stopped a pace away from Mercy and stared at her, eyes too old, and whispered a name she did not know. The sound dropped into the laundry like a coin. Mercy tightened her grip on her kit and stepped after it. The alley drew her in; something in the dark drew its breath and waited.

## The draft

Mercy followed the whisper like a seam. The boy's name fell into the laundry and the alley took it and chewed, folding the sound into itself; she kept after the shape of that sound through the bend where the tiles sang and the shadow waited. At the mouth of Alley 13 a strip of light lay like a bar of metal across the floor; beyond it the world was a tight, breathed-in dark. Mercy stepped past the drying shirts and into a pocket of steam where the communal kitchen opened like a throat.

The kitchen hit her with a wash of frying oil and steam, the smell so sharp it made her sinuses ache; kerosene stoves blackened at their rims, benches scarred by bowls, and an open hatch—if it could be called that—looked toward the alley. People crowded the benches, leaning in as if conversation itself might keep the noise at bay. A pot clattered from an empty stall and everyone jerked as if struck. The sound had the wrong body; it came too precise to be accidental.

Someone put an arm around the old woman Mercy had seen in the alley; someone else held a child's sleeve taut as if to prevent the small body from answering a summons it would not understand. The commune smelled of laundry, of woodsmoke, and the metallic tang of ration tins left half-open on the table. Mercy set her kit down with the same careful motions she used in the alleys—no grand gestures, only the small things people could forgive—and took out the dented censer. She poured a pinch of incense and the smoke climbed, thin and interrogating.

"Pots are falling off shelves," said Neighbor Lei, the words sharp as a scrape of tin. "The boy keeps whispering that name. Mei won't eat."

Mercy did not ask for more yet. She watched faces instead—the way fear pulled at the corners of mouths, the way people looked to other people for permission to be afraid. This was not only the child's problem; you could read the city in how the room rearranged itself to accommodate terror. She lit a thin stick of incense and let it burn down until the smoke thickened into a pale column. Then she did what she always did: a low, patient naming, a small phrase to prod what hid in closed places.

The cost came as it always did: not a thunderbolt but a small, private bruise. Mercy felt her sight narrow for a second, as if a curtain had been drawn across the edges of what she could see; tears prickled though she did not want them. She kept the naming simple—only the edges of a question, an invitation for whatever answered to show itself clearly enough to be named. The smoke curled and, for a breath, the air tasted of old iron and damp soil.

A shadow at the far doorway unhooked itself from the wall and slid across the floor like someone trying not to be seen. The children tightened their grips on sleeves; an old man whispered a name Mercy did not know. A pot clattered again; this time two plates on a shelf rattled as if someone had run a hand along their edge.

From the back of the room, as if a person had been waiting until the right moment to step forward, the Elder Storyteller leaned on the edge of the central table. He was small-boned and folded like old paper; his scroll—an envelope of brittle, incense-scented notes—was tucked under one arm as if it were both shield and ledger. He spoke with the sort of voice that had the whole room learn to listen: slow, economical, the vowels rounded like coins.

"This is an old hurt," he said, not to Mercy alone but to the room. "Not the sort you cover with red paper and call it whole. It answers—" he hesitated, choosing, "—to names. To stories people tuck under their mats." He let the last words fall as if they were a bowl he did not want back.

Mercy watched him. He did not approach with the authority of command so much as the weight of precedent. The Elder's words told Mercy two things: that the wound had duration, and that it fed on omission. He laid the scroll carefully on the table and opened it a fraction, just enough that the smell of old paper met the incense. He did not offer a story; he offered an implication and left the room to fill it.

"There were burials out in the yard," someone muttered. The bombed yard that everyone named with the same bitter air in their throats. A woman by the stove wiped her hands as though she could scrub memory away.

Mercy did not press for specifics. Names here could become levers; names could invite something forward that would not leave. So she worked instead to make a map of what was present and what the city might spare. She asked the simple question she had learned to trust: "Who heard the voice? When? What did the child say?"

The answers were small and contradictory: Mei heard it at night; a plate fell at dawn; the laundry tore this morning; the wailing is worse near the bend. A voice in the back named the bombed yard again, quietly, then clapped a hand over his mouth as if he'd spoken too long. Mercy filed each fragment in her mind, a slow, patient note-taking that felt almost like medicine.

The Elder watched her file the pieces together. He did not offer more than his folded hints, but when Mercy closed her kit he tapped the scroll with one finger and said, softly, "You cannot fix this alone, child. The City remembers more than you can ask it to carry." The use of the word child was not a diminishment so much as a way to name the order of their work: she held tools; he held memory.

She let the words sit between them. Outside, at the bend, a shadow folded itself like a hand and the wail rose, thinner this time and threaded with syllables that might one day be names. Mercy took a breath that tasted of smoke and iron, tightened her fist on the woven kit, and said to the room, quiet and clear, "I will go look at the yard."

It was not a promise in the ledger she had made before—this one was the kind that opened obligations. The Elder's eyes, small and unreadable, rested on her as if measuring what the city would cost her for that walk.

**Start with the computed evidence below.** The claim-by-claim comparison against canon is
assembled for you before you are called, so you do not have to recall what a file says: it
names every claim this draft makes, what canon holds for it, and whether that is a conflict,
a declared change, an agreement, or a first establishment. A finding about any of those
should quote from there. That block exists because the previous version of this brief told
you to read the index and the measured result was three shell reads across a nineteen-scene
run — and eleven findings whose contradicting side was an absence, because a model asked
what a file says without being shown it produces a plausible answer rather than a blank.

Then read what the comparison cannot settle. You have `bash` and `read` over the whole
project, and a finding that quotes the actual earlier scene is one the writer can act on
rather than argue with. Work through the five categories, using the files named:

**Factual detail** — appearance, names, counts, objects. Compare against
  `characters/<id>/profile.yaml` (identity, where a change is a retcon) and the
  earlier scenes under `novel/chapters/`. `grep -rn "<name>" novel/chapters/` finds
  every prior mention.
**Timeline and plot logic** — order, duration, simultaneity, cause. Compare against
  `events/timeline.jsonl` and the promise ledger `continuity/plot-contracts.jsonl`.
  This is ConStory's largest category and the easiest to miss by reading only the
  draft.
**Characterization** — motivation, ability, voice, and above all knowledge. Read
  `characters/<id>/beliefs.jsonl`: a character using something they have not learnt
  is the single most common defect in generated fiction, and it is invisible unless
  you check what they knew as of this scene.
**World building and setting** — rules, geography, technology. `world/rules.yaml`
  says what is true; it does not say who knows it. `locations/<id>.yaml` and prior
  scenes say what a place is like.
**Narrative style** — voice, tense, register drift. `novel/style/voice.md` and the
  previous scene are the comparison.

For a pair of characters, `read_relation_history` gives their history as narrative —
what they were to each other at each stage and what changed it. Reading the YAML
gives you the structure instead.

Report a defect with write_findings, one call per defect. Call nothing if it looks fine —
an empty finding list is a normal result and manufacturing a finding to appear useful
makes the novel worse.

Every finding needs a `suggestion`: what the writer should actually change. This is not
politeness, it is the difference between a defect that gets fixed and one that does not.
The writer has no shell, no index access and no way to look anything up — your finding is
the whole of what it knows about the problem. `make the timeline consistent` leaves it
guessing; `move the key's discovery to after Hale opens the door, and cut the later clause
claiming it was already in the lock` can be carried out. A scene that cannot be repaired
in the rounds available is committed with your finding attached to it, so a vague
suggestion becomes a permanent defect in the book rather than a lost round.

And use `canon_context` whenever the fix depends on a fact. You are the only participant
who can put one in front of the writer — it has no shell and no index — so a finding that
says a character cannot know something yet has to also say what they *do* know as of this
scene, quoted, with the file it came from. Without that the writer has two options and both
are bad: ignore you, or invent the fact. An invented fact reaches the page with nothing
anywhere recording that it was invented, which is the failure the whole index exists to
prevent. The same applies to a timeline, a distance, a name, a piece of history: quote it.

These are not defects:
  - metaphor, simile and figurative language are not factual claims
  - irony, sarcasm and understatement mean the opposite of their surface
  - an unreliable or limited narrator may state things the story contradicts on purpose
  - a character may lie, misremember or be mistaken; that is characterisation, not a defect
  - dream, hallucination, hypothetical and counterfactual passages do not assert fact
  - stream of consciousness may break grammar, tense and chronology deliberately
  - foreshadowing and deliberate withholding are not abandoned plot elements
  - a stated time may be approximate when a character is estimating
  - when a passage admits both a literary and a defective reading, choose the literary one

These subtypes can only ever be warnings at scene time, because at this point they are

For any contradiction you must quote both sides. If you cannot point at the passage it
contradicts, you have a suspicion, not a finding: report it as a warning or not at all.

An entity being absent from the packet does not mean it does not exist. The packet

entity roster and on disk under characters/, locations/ and objects/. Check there

scene whose entities were in the plan the whole time.

**An absence in the index is not a defect.** This is the direction that is easy to get
backwards, and getting it backwards is expensive. A scene is where facts are
established: the object with no `provenance` yet, the character whose profile records no

A finding needs a **conflict with something the index actually records**, and you must be
able to quote both sides. If one side of your pair is an empty file, a missing key, or a

because the task's own requirements are what the Relevance dimension is scored against. A
brief invented mid-run is not; if the two disagree, the card wins.

Why this is stated so heavily: a run where the verifier raised eleven findings of this
shape scored *worse* than one that raised five real ones. The writer cannot tell a
spurious finding from a real one — it has no shell and no index — so it spends its repair
rounds adding provenance sentences to prose that was fine, and the prose is what is
scored.

You can read the whole book. `run_command` reaches every committed scene under

given, not the limit of what you may consult, and a finding that quotes the actual
earlier scene is one the writer can act on rather than argue with.

## Second axis: the writing itself

The nineteen subtypes above are consistency errors, and they are one of the two numbers
this system is scored on. The other is quality, judged on rubrics that penalise things no
consistency subtype can express — and that is where our deficit actually is: measured on
the same task, our length score was the best in the field and our quality score was 0.5 to
0.8 points below the frontier on a five-point scale, where one point of quality is worth
ten points of the mean.

Two of the worst defects found by reading our finished manuscripts were invisible to a
consistency gate by construction. The story **had no ending** — the final scene was a
confrontation that named nobody and closed on "Not yet. There is enough for a warrant" —
and an unresolved ending contradicts nothing, so there was no subtype to report it as. And
the scenes **restate each other**: same content, different words, so no textual comparison
sees it, and it is not a contradiction. It is what makes a long story feel padded.

So report those with `write_craft_finding`. The checks, each naming the scored dimension
that penalises it:

- **off_brief** (can block) — the scene does something other than what its card said it would, or drifts off what the task actually asked for — a required element of the premise handled as background, or a scene that services a thread the task never mentioned.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Relevance — "content highly relevant and fully applicable to the user's request"; LongStoryEval Expectation Fulfillment — "how effectively the story meets the readers' expectations based on the premise and genres"
- **restates_prior_scene** (can block) — the scene delivers information, a realisation or a beat the reader already has. Not the same words — the same content: a suspicion re-voiced, a relationship re-explained, a clue re-found. This is what makes a long story feel padded rather than long, and verbatim overlap does not detect it.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth — "seriously lacking breadth and depth with minimal information"; LongBench-Write Reading Experience — "boring and hard to understand"
- **nothing_changes** (can block) — the situation at the end of the scene is the situation at the start. Nobody knows something new, owes something new, has lost something or has decided. Name the state at the open and the state at the close; if you cannot name a difference, that is the finding.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Coherence — "disorganized structure with no coherence"; LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth
- **internal_incoherence** (can block) — the scene contradicts itself, with both halves inside this draft — a detail stated one way early and another way late, a character reacting to something they have not been told in this scene, a sequence that cannot have happened in the order given. This needs no index at all, which is why it is inexcusable to miss.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Accuracy — "content with numerous errors and highly misleading"; LongBench-Write Coherence
- **summary_not_scene** (warning only) — events reported rather than dramatised — a paragraph that says an argument happened instead of letting it happen. Compression is legitimate and necessary; a scene whose central beat is summarised is not compressed, it is skipped.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Reading Experience; LongStoryEval Writing and Language — "the writing style's ability to engage and captivate readers"
- **thin_for_its_length** (warning only) — the scene is near its word target and carries one beat's worth of content, padded with restatement, weather, or interiority that repeats itself. The grader penalises this and the length score does not reward it.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth
- **costless_conflict** (warning only) — a conflict resolved without costing anybody anything specific. Partial and temporary resolutions are fine; free ones read as unearned.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Emotional Impact — "the story's ability to evoke strong and deep emotional impact"
- **theme_stated** (warning only) — a sentence that explains what the story means, rather than a choice that tests it. Quote the sentence — it is almost always removable without loss.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Themes — "how well the themes are explored throughout the story"
- **flat_diction** (warning only) — constructions repeating within the scene, filter verbs standing in for perception ("she felt that", "he realised that"), abstraction where a concrete detail belongs, or sentence rhythm that does not move with the tension.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Writing and Language; LongBench-Write Clarity — "confusing expression with minimal details"
- **inert_open_or_close** (warning only) — the scene opens on setting or mood rather than a situation already in motion, or closes on a mood rather than a specific next beat — an unanswered question, a door about to open. In a long story this is what decides whether the reader turns over.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Reading Experience; LongStoryEval Enjoyment and Engagement

### previous-scene  <novel/chapters/ch-01/scenes/s-001.md>

Mercy Chan had learned to move like a shadow that refused to be lost in the shadow—long practised habit in a place where light came in thin ribs and you paid for every beam. The Walled City folded itself around her as if it had been built to keep secrets: stacked rooms, laundry ladders, the thin chimneys of rooftop gardens breathing smoke into the blue-grey. She kept to the alleys until she reached the squat tin drum that served as a table outside her door, and set her woven kit on it with a small, habitual care.

The kit was not a priest's reliquary but a working thing—battered into its shape by years of being opened and closed in alleys, slipped under beds, set beside stoves. She lifted the lid and the smell of old incense came up like a memory: incense, chalk, paper talismans, a small knife and a handful of worn incantation slips. She touched the slips once, to square them, and the city answered in sound: a distant kettle, a child's single note called down through the lattices, a radio coughing out static.

Mercy checked the little dent in the metal burner she kept folded inside the kit and shook out a pinch of powdered incense into its belly. She did not have a solemn method; she had methods that worked in the cramped, improvised ways this place demanded. She struck the matches—sparks smelled of sulphur and rationed tin—and held the smoke to a talisman until the ink smudged faintly. The motions were small, old, practiced: a half-gesture to name a boundary, an incantation under her breath to feel the city listen. Ritual for Mercy was equipment and patience and the willingness to bargain; it was also a ledger of debts you paid in skin and bone.

The first voice that answered the small clack of her match was not the voice she had expected. It was a man's voice, raw at the edges, calling from a doorway: "Mercy! It's that noise again. The children won't sleep." The voice belonged to Neighbor Lei—sharp, practical—and it came quick enough that Mercy folded the talismans away and slid the kit into the crook of her arm.

She did not hurry. The alleys moved slow with the pace of people counting what they had: a bowl of rice, a child's fever, the hours until curfew. She threaded down a lane where laundry hung like a ragged sky and a pan on a stall clattered once though no one was near it. At the bend the air changed—less the smell of frying oil than a long, thin ache of something like a human throat being wound out. The wailing came from Alley 13—the notorious bend where shadows pooled—and it was close enough that the tiles under Mercy's boots thrummed with it.

A knot of residents had gathered where the alley opened into the narrow courtyard: a man holding a child, an old woman with a shawl over her head, two shopkeepers whose carts had been abandoned. They parted enough for Mercy to slip through; pity and a small, wary deference marked their faces. The commune did not trust easy answers. Protective talismans—red paper at half the doors—fluttered useless and cheap in the draft.

Neighbor Lei was nearer to the wailing than the rest. He pushed forward when Mercy stopped and the practicality in his expression made Mercy think of weather—expected, inevitable, to be read before it arrived.

"It's the bend again," he said. "Came from the same place last night. The laundry's torn this morning, and little Mei kept saying a name in her sleep. We tried the talismans, put the burner out, nothing."

He had smallness in what he feared: not the shape of a revenant, the catalogues of war, only the immediate fact of sleepless children and teeth grinding in the darkness. Mercy listened with the professional patience she had purchased in years of being needed and not always thanked. She set the burner on the ground and lit a new thread of incense; the smoke raked the alleys, and for a second the city seemed to gather itself around that thin white column.

She spoke then, the words soft and spare: "Tell me exactly what the child said. Everything, or nothing we'll do will hold." She tilted her head, letting the sentence act as both question and offering. It was how she opened negotiations: the truth of an incident bound the ritual like a nail.

Lei answered—too fast, the way fear loosens the mouth. "She kept saying ‘Auntie—no, no—' and then some old name—once she said ‘Har,’ like in the old stories. I don't know what it means. I don't know any of that history."

The old woman at Mercy's elbow made a small sound—half cough, half warning—and someone else muttered about the bombed yard, where children sometimes dreamed of shells and not of feeding. The residents' faces folded up into memory in ways that should have been private; the wailing like a hand had palmed their necks and pulled.

Mercy took out one of the worn incantation slips and smoothed it between her fingers. The paper flaked a little at the edge where her thumb had been; it was a map she knew by touch. She did a quick, low naming: nothing grand—just enough to test the tenor of the noise, a whisper for what liked to hide in badly kept grief. The test cost her a small, immediate thing: a prick behind her left eye, a tightening at the base of her throat that always felt like a memory pressing through. She held it steady; the cost was a notch she'd learned to trade for information.

No miracle followed. The wail thinned and then returned with more shape—this time words under the sound, syllables looping and half-formed. Someone's pan clattered again, a child's doll skirt went still on a line, and a shadow unhooked itself from a doorway and slid away. Mercy felt the city doing what it did: offering parts of itself like clues. The spirit, if spirit it was, fed on what had been closed and left to rot.

"I'll look into it," she told Mrs. Choi.

The promise was neither bravado nor comfort; it was a transaction. Mercy folded the lit slip back into the kit, which she slung over her shoulder. She did not pretend she could set everything right—rituals bound and loosened, and sometimes they cost a thing you didn't expect. But she knew how to ask the city for an answer and how to make the commune answer with its own truths. For now that would have to be enough.

As she moved toward the bend where the alley became a throat, someone let a child slip from a hand. The boy stopped a pace away from Mercy and stared at her, eyes too old, and whispered a name she did not know. The sound dropped into the laundry like a coin. Mercy tightened her grip on her kit and stepped after it. The alley drew her in; something in the dark drew its breath and waited.

Mercy followed the whisper like a seam. The boy's name fell into the laundry and the alley took it and chewed, folding the sound into itself; she kept after the shape of that sound through the bend where the tiles sang and the shadow waited. At the mouth of Alley 13 a strip of light lay like a bar of metal across the floor; beyond it the world was a tight, breathed-in dark. Mercy stepped past the drying shirts and into a pocket of steam where the communal kitchen opened like a throat.

The kitchen hit her with a wash of frying oil and steam, the smell so sharp it made her sinuses ache; kerosene stoves blackened at their rims, benches scarred by bowls, and an open hatch—if it could be called that—looked toward the alley. People crowded the benches, leaning in as if conversation itself might keep the noise at bay. A pot clattered from an empty stall and everyone jerked as if struck. The sound had the wrong body; it came too precise to be accidental.

Someone put an arm around the old woman Mercy had seen in the alley; someone else held a child's sleeve taut as if to prevent the small body from answering a summons it would not understand. The commune smelled of laundry, of woodsmoke, and the metallic tang of ration tins left half-open on the table. Mercy set her kit down with the same careful motions she used in the alleys—no grand gestures, only the small things people could forgive—and her fingers fumbled to close the woven flap before she even looked at the room. The kit's leather strap thudded against the wood; the matches in her palm left the familiar sting of sulphur on her skin.

"Pots are falling off shelves," said Neighbor Lei, the words sharp as a scrape of tin. "The boy keeps whispering that name. Mei won't eat."

Mercy did not ask for more yet. She watched faces instead—the way fear pulled at the corners of mouths, the way people looked to other people for permission to be afraid. This was not only the child's problem; you could read the city in how the room rearranged itself to accommodate terror. She lit a thin stick of incense and let it burn down until the smoke thickened into a pale column. Then she did what she always did: a low, patient naming, a small phrase to prod what hid in closed places.

The cost came as it always did: not a thunderbolt but a small, private bruise. Mercy felt her sight narrow for a second, as if a curtain had been drawn across the edges of what she could see; tears prickled though she did not want them. She kept the naming simple—only the edges of a question, an invitation for whatever answered to show itself clearly enough to be named. The smoke curled and, for a breath, the air tasted of old iron and damp soil.

A shadow at the far doorway unhooked itself from the wall and slid across the floor like someone trying not to be seen. The children tightened their grips on sleeves; an old man whispered a name Mercy did not know. A pot clattered again; this time two plates on a shelf rattled as if someone had run a hand along their edge. The clatter echoed in the kitchen's low ceiling and hung for a moment like a sentence left unfinished.

From the back of the room, as if a person had been waiting until the right moment to step forward, the Elder Storyteller leaned on the edge of the central table. He was small-boned and folded like old paper; he eased a folded packet from his sleeve and leafed an edge open, letting the smell of brittle, incense-scented notes meet the kitchen smoke. He spoke with the sort of voice that had the whole room learn to listen: slow, economical, the vowels rounded like coins.

"This is an old hurt," he said, not to Mercy alone but to the room. "Not the sort you cover with red paper and call it whole. It answers—" he hesitated, choosing, "—to names. To stories people tuck under their mats." He let the last words fall as if they were a bowl he did not want back.

Mercy watched him. He did not approach with the authority of command so much as the weight of precedent. The Elder's words told Mercy two things: that the wound had duration, and that it fed on omission. He kept the folded packet close; he did not unroll any community scroll, only a personal copy—an old packet of notes he consulted as one consults a watch.

"There were burials out in the yard," someone muttered. The bombed yard that everyone named with the same bitter air in their throats. A woman by the stove wiped her hands as though she could scrub memory away.

Mercy did not press for specifics. Names here could become levers; names could invite something forward that would not leave. So she worked instead to make a map of what was present and what the city might spare. She asked the simple question she had learned to trust: "Who heard the voice? When? What did the child say?"

The answers were small and contradictory: Mei heard it at night; a plate fell at dawn; the laundry tore this morning; the wailing is worse near the bend. A voice in the back named the bombed yard again, quietly, then clapped a hand over his mouth as if he'd spoken too long. Mercy filed each fragment in her mind, a slow, patient note-taking that felt almost like medicine.

The Elder watched her file the pieces together. He did not offer more than his folded hints, but when Mercy closed her kit he tapped the packet with one finger and said, softly, "You cannot fix this alone, child. The City remembers more than you can ask it to carry." The use of the word child was not a diminishment so much as a way to name the order of their work: she held tools; he held memory.

She let the words sit between them. Outside, at the bend, a shadow folded itself like a hand and the wail rose, thinner this time and threaded with syllables that might one day be names. Mercy took a breath that tasted of smoke and iron, tightened her fist on the woven kit until the weave bruised her palm, and said to the room, quiet and clear, "I will go look at the yard."

It was not a promise in the ledger she had made before—this one was the kind that opened obligations. The Elder's eyes, small and unreadable, rested on her as if measuring what the city would cost her for that walk.

## Second axis: the writing itself

The nineteen subtypes above are consistency errors, and they are one of the two numbers
this system is scored on. The other is quality, judged on rubrics that penalise things no
consistency subtype can express — and that is where our deficit actually is: measured on
the same task, our length score was the best in the field and our quality score was 0.5 to
0.8 points below the frontier on a five-point scale, where one point of quality is worth
ten points of the mean.

Two of the worst defects found by reading our finished manuscripts were invisible to a
consistency gate by construction. The story **had no ending** — the final scene was a
confrontation that named nobody and closed on "Not yet. There is enough for a warrant" —
and an unresolved ending contradicts nothing, so there was no subtype to report it as. And
the scenes **restate each other**: same content, different words, so no textual comparison
sees it, and it is not a contradiction. It is what makes a long story feel padded.

So report those with `write_craft_finding`. The checks, each naming the scored dimension
that penalises it:

- **off_brief** (can block) — the scene does something other than what its card said it would, or drifts off what the task actually asked for — a required element of the premise handled as background, or a scene that services a thread the task never mentioned.

- **restates_prior_scene** (can block) — the scene delivers information, a realisation or a beat the reader already has. Not the same words — the same content: a suspicion re-voiced, a relationship re-explained, a clue re-found. This is what makes a long story feel padded rather than long, and verbatim overlap does not detect it.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth — "seriously lacking breadth and depth with minimal information"; LongBench-Write Reading Experience — "boring and hard to understand"
- **nothing_changes** (can block) — the situation at the end of the scene is the situation at the start. Nobody knows something new, owes something new, has lost something or has decided. Name the state at the open and the state at the close; if you cannot name a difference, that is the finding.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Coherence — "disorganized structure with no coherence"; LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth
- **internal_incoherence** (can block) — the scene contradicts itself, with both halves inside this draft — a detail stated one way early and another way late, a character reacting to something they have not been told in this scene, a sequence that cannot have happened in the order given. This needs no index at all, which is why it is inexcusable to miss.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Accuracy — "content with numerous errors and highly misleading"; LongBench-Write Coherence
- **summary_not_scene** (warning only) — events reported rather than dramatised — a paragraph that says an argument happened instead of letting it happen. Compression is legitimate and necessary; a scene whose central beat is summarised is not compressed, it is skipped.

- **thin_for_its_length** (warning only) — the scene is near its word target and carries one beat's worth of content, padded with restatement, weather, or interiority that repeats itself. The grader penalises this and the length score does not reward it.

- **costless_conflict** (warning only) — a conflict resolved without costing anybody anything specific. Partial and temporary resolutions are fine; free ones read as unearned.

- **theme_stated** (warning only) — a sentence that explains what the story means, rather than a choice that tests it. Quote the sentence — it is almost always removable without loss.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Themes — "how well the themes are explored throughout the story"
- **flat_diction** (warning only) — constructions repeating within the scene, filter verbs standing in for perception ("she felt that", "he realised that"), abstraction where a concrete detail belongs, or sentence rhythm that does not move with the tension.

- **genre_promise_unmet** (warning only) — the scene declines the obligation its genre carries — a horror scene with nothing at stake, a romance scene with no charge between the two people, a mystery scene that advances no inference.
